title: SAT Scores: 400–1600 and What Colleges Want
summary: How the 400–1600 score is built, what counts as a strong score, and how test-optional policies change the calculus.

nodes.label: Percentiles
nodes.note: How you rank vs other test-takers

nodes.label: Test-optional
nodes.note: Many US colleges don't require the SAT

chunks.heading: How the score is built
chunks.body: Your total is the **sum of two section scores — Reading and Writing (200–800) and Math (200–800) — for a 400–1600 total**. Each section score comes from your performance across **both modules** (harder questions earn more), not a simple right-answer count.
chunks.realExample: Because harder questions weigh more, two students with the same number correct can get different section scores if one answered the tougher adaptive items — accuracy on hard questions pays.
chunks.memoryHook: RW + Math, each 200–800 → 400–1600. Hard questions are worth more.

chunks.heading: What's a strong score?
chunks.body: Judge your score by **percentile and by your target colleges**, not a universal bar. Very roughly, **1200+ is above average, 1400+ is competitive for selective universities, and 1500+ for the most selective**. Always check the **middle-50% range** your specific colleges publish.
chunks.realExample: A 1450 is strong for many universities but only mid-range at the most selective ones — look up each college's middle-50% SAT range to see where you stand for THAT school.
chunks.memoryHook: 1200+ above average, 1400+ selective, 1500+ elite — but check each college's own range.

chunks.heading: Test-optional changes the game
chunks.body: Many US universities are **test-optional**, meaning you can apply without an SAT. A **strong score still helps** (and some scholarships use it), but a weak score can be **left off**. Decide per college whether submitting helps or hurts your application.
chunks.realExample: If your SAT is at or above a college's middle-50%, submit it; if it's below, a test-optional college may prefer you don't — check each school's policy before deciding.
chunks.memoryHook: Test-optional: submit if your score helps, withhold if it doesn't. Decide per college.

chunks.heading: Retakes, superscoring and no penalty
chunks.body: There's **no penalty for wrong answers**, so answer everything. You can **retake the SAT**, and many colleges **superscore** (best section scores across dates) — so a focused retake to lift your weaker section is often the fastest way to raise your total.
chunks.realExample: Weaker in Math? A retake that lifts only Math, combined with superscoring, raises your effective total without needing to re-ace Reading & Writing.
chunks.memoryHook: No penalty, retakes allowed, superscoring common — target your weaker section.

recall.q: How is the SAT total score calculated?
recall.a: It's the sum of two section scores — Reading and Writing (200–800) and Math (200–800) — for a 400–1600 total.

recall.q: Why can two students with the same number correct get different section scores?
recall.a: Because harder adaptive questions are worth more, so accuracy on tougher items raises the section score.

recall.q: Roughly what SAT totals count as above-average, selective and elite?
recall.a: About 1200+ above average, 1400+ competitive for selective universities, and 1500+ for the most selective — but check each college's middle-50% range.

recall.q: What does 'test-optional' mean for submitting your SAT?
recall.a: You can apply without it; submit a strong score that helps, and consider withholding a weak one — decide per college.

recall.q: How can superscoring help on a retake?
recall.a: Many colleges take your best section scores across dates, so a retake lifting only your weaker section can raise your effective total.
